steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on identifying which parts of a learning robot's architecture need to be explained to users. Motivate it with everyday robots that users train, explain how users' misconceptions hurt interactive learning, and give an overview of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Robots in everyday life and the need to personalize them
- Interactive task learning from user feedback
- Misconceptions in users' mental models and their effects
- Explaining the architecture, but only the needed parts
- Overview of the paper

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text: More and more robots are part of our everyday lives. For example there is Paro in the care sector, DaVinci in the operating room, temi in hospitals, Pepper in retail, and iRobot vacuum cleaners in our homes, to name only a few. If there are robots in our immediate environment that support us in everyday tasks, they should be adapted to our personal preferences. So the users need to train the robots to customize them to their needs. This training is done during a human-robot interaction. One common and effective method for this training is interactive task learning. This method uses the feedback of the user for the learning process, for example by using human feedback directly as a reward or by demonstration. Different approaches for this have been presented in several earlier works. These methods depend on how informative the user's feedback is. They can suffer if the users have misconceptions in their mental model of how the robot works inside. This phenomenon has been examined in prior work. For example, if the robot has human features like eyes and is taught by demonstration, then when the robot does not know what the user wants or expects, the user tends to make extra movements so the robot can follow better. Other researchers found this movement behavior in their studies. These movements might then be learned as part of the target movement, and this slows down the learning process. Another example of these misconceptions, in learning based on direct reward, is that the reward is misused for motivation, which overweights the graded behavior, as was shown in earlier work. A natural way to resolve these misconceptions is to explain the inner lying architecture of the robot. But the inner structures of the robot can be very complex. Also, users are not willing to invest a lot of time in training the robot. So the best option would be to only explain the parts of the robot's architecture or algorithm that the user misunderstood or that are missing in their mental model, so that the training is not frustrating and is successful as fast as possible. This was indicated in a previous paper. Therefore a structured procedure is needed to identify these parts of the architecture. In this paper we present our approach and how it was developed. First we introduce the related work on explainability in human-robot interaction and on mental models. We worked out our approach using a robot and algorithm architecture as an example, and we present this example architecture in section 2.2. After that, in section 3, we present how we worked out this approach and how the elaborated steps apply to our example architecture. Finally, we summarize and discuss our approach and present future work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In our everyday lives, we come into contact with more and more robots. For example, Paro by [1] in the care sector, DaVinci by [2] in the operating room, temi by [3] in hospitals, Pepper by [4] in retail, and iRobot vacuum cleaners by [5] in our homes, to name only a few. If we have robots in our immediate environment that support us in everyday tasks, they should be adapted to our personal preferences. Therefore, users must train the robots to customize them to their needs. This is done by training during a human-robot interaction. One common and effective method for such training is interactive task learning [6]. This method uses the user's feedback for the learning process, for example directly by using human feedback as a reward or by demonstration. Different approaches for this were presented by [7], [8], and [9]. Those methods thus depend on the informativeness of the user's feedback, and they can suffer if users have misconceptions within their mental model of the inner functioning of the robot. This phenomenon was examined by [10]. For example, if the robot has human features like eyes and is taught by demonstration, when the robot does not know what the user wants or expects, the user tends to make extra movements so that the robot can follow better. [11] found this movement behavior in their studies. These movements might then be learned as part of the target movement, slowing down the learning process. Another example of these misconceptions in learning based on direct reward is the misuse of the reward for motivation, which overweights the graded behavior, as shown by [7]. A natural approach to resolve those misconceptions is to explain the inner lying architecture of the robot [7]. However, these inner structures of the robot can be very complex, and users are not willing to invest a lot of time into training the robot. Therefore, the best option would be to explain only those parts of the robot's architecture or algorithm that the user misunderstood or is missing in their mental model, such that training is not frustrating and is successful as quickly as possible. This was indicated in the paper by [12]. Hence, a structured procedure is needed to identify these parts of the architecture. In this paper, we present our approach and its development. First, we introduce the related work in the field of explainability in human-robot interaction and mental models. We worked out our approach using a robot and algorithm architecture as an example, which we present in section 2.2. Afterward, in section 3, we present how we worked out this approach and the application of the elaborated steps to our exemplary architecture. Lastly, we summarize and discuss our approach and present future work.
